name: 标题 1
text: Research Background
textPreview: Research Background

name: 内容占位符 2
text:
Search engines typically present users with multiple sources, links, and evidentiary cues.
Generative AI increasingly organizes information as “direct answer → integrated explanation → follow-up questions.”
Research problem: At the group level, if many members rely on the same model, similar training data, the same retrieval system, and similar answer-generation logic, their seemingly independent judgments may contain the same omissions, narrative frames, and errors. The number of judgments continues to grow, but the number of independent information samples does not grow proportionally.
Real-world examples include AI search assistants embedded in Weibo and WeChat.

textPreview: Research Background

name: 内容占位符 2
text:
DIRECT EVIDENCE ON AI-ASSISTED WISDOM OF CROWDS
• Pal, Palley & Satopää (2026), “Enhancing Crowd Accuracy in AI-Assisted Judgmental Forecasting.” The same AI advice is shared information that can be counted repeatedly and overrepresented when judgments are averaged. Across three experiments (N = 3,188), the authors propose correcting shared AI signals with participants’ pre-AI judgments.
• Schoenegger et al. (2024), “AI-Augmented Predictions: LLM Assistants Improve Human Forecasting Accuracy.” Among 991 participants answering six forecasting questions, access to an assigned LLM improved individual accuracy by 24%–28%. The study also tests whether lower judgment diversity harms the wisdom of crowds.
BOUNDARY
AI may have only a small average effect on each member, yet a shared model can expose members to similar evidence, frames, and arguments. This raises error correlation and weakens collective intelligence based on independent judgment. This boundary is consistent with Artificial Hivemind: repeated outputs from the same model and outputs across models were homogeneous, but the study measured model responses—not human political attitudes or organizational decisions.

name: 标题 1
text: Research Gaps
textPreview: Research Gaps

name: 内容占位符 2
text:
GAP 1 — Existing work largely stops at the model-output layer
Artificial Hivemind and related error studies show that LLM responses may be similar, but not how this similarity becomes human information selection, belief updating, and group-level judgment.
GAP 2 — Individual and group accuracy are often conflated
Studies commonly ask whether AI improves individual judgment, but rarely whether higher judgment correlation reduces aggregation gains even when average individual quality is unchanged or improved.
GAP 3 — Traditional opinion dynamics lacks an interactive generative source
Traditional models focus on interpersonal averaging, imitation, and selective exposure. An LLM combines a shared model prior with user-conditioned output: it may repeat similar content to everyone or generate different content by user position. This shared-base/personalized-output structure remains under-modeled.

name: 标题 1
text: Theoretical Framework
textPreview: Theoretical Framework

name: 内容占位符 2
text:
WISDOM OF CROWDS AND THE DIVERSITY PREDICTION THEOREM

Wisdom of crowds (Surowiecki, 2004)
Collective judgment outperforms individual judgment under three necessary conditions: diverse views, independent decisions, and dispersed private information. A common AI reference signal directly weakens independence and diversity.

Diversity prediction theorem (Page, 2007)
Group error = average individual error − predictive diversity.
AI can improve individual accuracy while reducing predictive diversity. These forces work in opposite directions. As group size grows, the weight of diversity rises; eventually, the loss of diversity may outweigh the gain in individual accuracy.

Social influence and diversity (Lorenz et al., 2011)
A common external signal makes individual judgments converge and can weaken group forecasting. This study treats uniform AI advice as a global external signal and tests whether it actually reduces collective predictive performance.

title: Research Question: Do LLMs Undermine the Wisdom of Crowds?

name: 标题 1
text: Research Question: Do LLMs Undermine the Wisdom of Crowds?
textPreview: Research Question: Do LLMs Undermine the Wisdom of Crowds?

name: 内容占位符 2
text:
When individuals with heterogeneous initial positions independently and repeatedly interact with an LLM about the same public-policy issue, how does output homogeneity change the correlation structure of group judgment?

“Correlation structure” includes three possible outcomes:
• convergence in information samples;
• higher correlation in judgment errors;
• convergence, persistent division, or further polarization of opinions.

When information quality and average individual accuracy are broadly comparable, does a shared LLM increase error correlation across members, thereby reducing the group’s effective amount of independent information and the quality of collective judgment?

MODEL-OUTPUT HOMOGENEITY → CORRELATED INFORMATION EXPOSURE → BELIEF UPDATING → GROUP JUDGMENT STRUCTURE

name: 内容占位符 2
text:
H1. A shared LLM increases the similarity of information obtained by members.

H2. A shared LLM increases correlation in members’ judgment errors.

H3. A shared LLM reduces the accuracy gain produced by judgment aggregation.

H4. Model diversity mitigates the loss of crowd wisdom caused by a shared LLM.

H4 also serves as a mechanism test. If model diversity first reduces error correlation and then restores aggregation gains, the core mechanism is supported. If it only increases linguistic variation without changing error correlation or aggregation outcomes, the mechanism is not validated.

textPreview: Modeling Foundation

name: 内容占位符 2
text:
OPINION DYNAMICS: WHEN DOES A SHARED MODEL PRODUCE CONVERGENCE OR DIVERGENCE?

Traditional opinion dynamics studies how people update judgments from others’ opinions. DeGroot models convergence through weighted averaging; Friedkin–Johnsen allows attachment to initial positions; Hegselmann–Krause bounded confidence assumes that people accept only information sufficiently close to their current view, allowing multiple opinion clusters.

Here, opinion dynamics is not mainly used to simulate interpersonal diffusion. It describes how members with different initial positions update sequentially in response to shared—but potentially personalized—LLM information.

title: Opinion Dynamics Models Human Group Behavior

name: 标题 1
text: Opinion Dynamics Models Human Group Behavior
textPreview: Opinion Dynamics Models Human Group Behavior

name: 内容占位符 2
text:
Opinion dynamics explains how users update their positions after receiving an LLM response.
Agent i’s opinion in round t is xᵢ,ₜ, and the policy position implied by the LLM response is sᵢ,ₜ. The basic update rule is:
xᵢ,ₜ₊₁ = (1 − λᵢ)xᵢ,ₜ + λᵢsᵢ,ₜ
where λᵢ is the agent’s reliance on the LLM.

With bounded confidence, the agent accepts only information within a threshold of its current view:
|sᵢ,ₜ − xᵢ,ₜ| ≤ τᵢ

This structure can produce two outcomes:
• similar answers from a shared model generate convergence;
• evidence selected by initial position gives opposing camps directionally different answers, generating division or polarization.

Sycophancy and personalization are therefore boundary conditions on the homogenizing effect of a shared model.

name: paper1-optimal-stopping-detail
text:
DETAILED EXPLANATION

Optimal stopping theory asks when a decision maker should stop when information or options arrive sequentially, continued observation is costly, and future gains are uncertain. Its core is not “more search is always better,” but a comparison between the expected marginal benefit and marginal cost of one more search.

Weitzman’s classic model converts search objects into reservation values. Search continues while an unchecked option still offers sufficient expected gain; it stops when the best observed outcome exceeds the reservation value of every unchecked option. Paper 1 is not exactly the same “find the best option” task, but it can use the central criterion: Is the expected information value of the next piece of evidence greater than the cost of obtaining it?

JUDGMENT AND DECISION MAKING (JDM)

The Journal of Behavioral Decision Making is a leading journal in this field, and the foundational roots of all these terms lie here:

Algorithm aversion
A signature JDM concept formally named in 2015, describing the cognitive bias of deliberately rejecting algorithmic advice that performs better.

Expectations and expertise
From cognitive psychology and behavioral decision research: expectation bias, overconfidence, and domain-expert bias are classic JDM variables.

Decision autonomy / decisional agency
A core decision-psychology concept linked to locus of control and the psychological need to retain control over decisions.

Cognitive compatibility
A cognitive-psychology and information-processing term comparing intuitive human processing with algorithmic logic.

Divergent rationalities
A term derived from the contrast between the heuristics-and-biases paradigm and fast-and-frugal ecological rationality, asking what counts as rational decision making.

text:
Research on trust in AI is highly interdisciplinary, involving psychology, philosophy, computer science, and other fields. Its theoretical foundations are correspondingly complex.

The literature covers general trust in artificial intelligence, human resistance to AI, AI in moral decision making, AI in managerial decisions, and trust in autonomous driving.

name: 标题 1
text: Defining Trust
textPreview: Defining Trust

name: 内容占位符 2
text:
The classic three-factor model of interpersonal trust proposes that trust and trustworthiness derive not only from perceived ability, but also from integrity and benevolence.

Trust in AI likewise has two dimensions: performance/capability (can it complete the task?) and morality (is the system directed toward good, and are its processes and purposes legitimate?). Research has not consistently separated performance trust from moral trust, and many studies conflate them. People care about both AI performance and its design intent, operating logic, benevolence, and fairness. An AI system can be highly capable but deceptive, stable but unethical, or morally aligned but inaccurate.

text: Research Gaps
textPreview: Research Gaps

name: 内容占位符 2
text:
• AI-governance research analyzes institutions but rarely measures individuals’ actual reliance.

• AI-trust research measures individual reliance, but often treats interface prompts, explanations, or labels as “governance,” without a real institutional basis.

• Research is scarce on person–context fit as a moderator of AI-system features. The effect of the same AI feature—explainability, anthropomorphism, or high accuracy—depends on whether users perceive the AI as fitting themselves and the task, yet this moderation is rarely examined directly.

• Much of the literature is cross-sectional and static rather than longitudinal. AI changes rapidly, so findings about conventional automation and early algorithms may lack temporal validity for current large models. Almost no work tracks how public trust changes over time with technological diffusion and social events.

text: Trust Calibration Bias

name: 内容占位符 2
text:
Perceptual calibration bias = subjectively judged AI reliability − actual reliability

Behavioral calibration bias = actual degree of reliance − the degree of reliance warranted by relative capability

Algorithm aversion and algorithm appreciation are therefore no longer isolated phenomena:
• underestimating AI capability is a negative perceptual bias;
• knowing AI is better but not adopting it is under-reliance;
• knowing AI is unreliable but continuing to use it is over-reliance.

Regulators should test different intervention combinations for different conditions so that user reliance approaches a reasonable level.

text: Practical Relevance
textPreview: Practical Relevance

name: 内容占位符 2
text:
For example, when will people think AI should be introduced into a particular stage?

In the past, this was simple: once an algorithm’s accuracy was high enough, including it in the decision process seemed natural. AI is different.

AI enters more complex human settings—not only settings where accuracy is measurable, but also consultation, emotional decisions, and others.

The framework must therefore expand and first clarify questions that past theories could not resolve:
How should traditional algorithms, AI, and humans be distinguished? How are these actors perceived differently?

name: 内容占位符 2
text:
Current theory has reached the claim that people believe AI clearly changes where responsibility is assigned.

The next question is whether responsibility assigned to AI resembles shifting blame to another human or the traditional shifting of blame to an algorithm.

Both types of responsibility transfer are theoretically mature. Yet many studies still treat AI as a conventional algorithm, which clearly cannot explain the emotional dependence that people sometimes develop toward AI.

Practical relevance: If we can show that responsibility transfer to AI follows a genuinely new path, the result will influence future ethics, law, and regulation.

name: 内容占位符 2
text:
Accountability theory argues that being observed, evaluated, and required to explain increases a person’s sense of accountability.

Responsibility/control theory argues that responsibility should be grounded in actual control, causal contribution, and decision authority.

AI systems can separate the two: a person may be required to sign, explain, and bear the consequences without genuinely forming or controlling the decision.

Work on meaningful human control explicitly argues that responsibility should be proportionate to actual control and authority. The “moral crumple zone” identifies how automated systems can concentrate failure responsibility on human operators with limited control.
